description: STRONG ADMISSION: the paper says that IT is or did a replication. Arms were chosen by the greedy set cover of `redesign/rulebook_v2.html` §1.1 and by marginal contribution, not by enumeration — six arms carry 92% of known replication studies and the thirty arms the v1 book carried on top of them bought 1%. One clause per arm so a diagnostics run can attribute every hit and each arm can be retired on its own count. Note what is NOT here. Bare `replications? of` is deliberately excluded: it is the highest-recall arm in the book (40.4% of positives) and also fires on 82.2% of screen-confirmed negatives, and no cheap syntactic anchor repairs it (§1.2) — it is replication-signal's last arm instead. `registered report of` is excluded because most Registered Reports are original studies. Reproduction vocabulary is out of scope entirely; it belongs to reproduction-signal and #155. OPEN SCOPE QUESTION (D3), landing on the `aim|set out to replicate` arm: if a planned-but-not-completed replication is not a FLoRA record, that arm belongs in replication-signal or in a pile of its own.

measured.sample: 2,895 distinct replication studies with a usable abstract from `data/FLoRA entry sheet - replication list.csv` (3,851 rows, 2,978 distinct doi_r), text = ref_r + abstract_r as a proxy for the pool row's title + abstract; scored against 501 rows of `data/not_a_replication.csv`, papers that passed the old filter, reached the two-voter screen and were judged not_a_replication. Computed 2026-08-04, proposal SS1 (redesign/rulebook_v2.html).
measured.rationale: With all twelve arms this rule fires on 82.6% of the positives at 6.8% of the false-positive load (80.8% / 6.2% without the four marginal arms). READ BOTH DENOMINATORS AS WHAT THEY ARE. The recall figure is an UPPER BOUND: a substantial share of the entry sheet was discovered by keyword search, so a phrase rule scored against it over-estimates recall, most for the arms that did the finding; the sheet's columns do not separate curated-list entries from pipeline-found ones, so this is corrected by the SS6 holdout design, not here. The 6.8% is NOT a population false-positive rate and must never be quoted as this rule's precision: the negatives corpus is the false-positive load itself — what the old loose filter admitted and the screen then rejected — so what it measures exactly is the composition of the money currently being wasted. Per-arm firing on the 501 negatives: `we replicat*` 1.6%, `replicate and extend` 1.6%, `replication study` 0.8%, `fail/attempt to replicate` 0.8%, `study replicated` 0.0%, the qualifier family 2.8%. The four marginal arms were measured MARGINALLY, i.e. what each adds once the arms above it are in: `success* replicat*` +26 positives / +2 negatives (13:1, and the only arm carrying the successful-outcome framing); the negation matrix +18 / +1; `replication attempt(s)` +8 / +0; the failure nouns +1 / +0. That last +1 is the clearest case on the page of why a marginal count is not a coverage argument: 'We present a failed replication of Smith (2009)' fires the noun arm and NOTHING ELSE in this rule, because 'replication' there is a noun and the sentence never uses the verb. It scores +1 only because in this keyword-assembled corpus the papers phrasing it that way almost all also say 'replication study' or 'we replicated' somewhere in the same abstract. A marginal count of +1 on a biased corpus is weak evidence of redundancy; a marginal count of +0 negatives is strong evidence of harmlessness, and when an arm is free the second number decides. The rule discards nothing — it admits into a tier that decides — so the evidence gate does not bind it; this entry documents the claim rather than satisfying a gate.
